research_concepts: derived play-type possession records in a graph database
label validation against foul, volume and identity benchmarks
methodological_questions: Can a preceding teammate DRIVE be identified reliably from the play-by-play, given that the play-type labels themselves have documented failures?
Does a preceding teammate DRIVE change PNR PPP after conditioning on the labeled possession and its context, or does the apparent effect come from labeling or outcome leakage?
Is there enough PNR and DRIVE-sequence exposure in the stated seasons for a powered comparison, and how do playoff and partial-season data affect that?
Which validation gates must pass before any sequential play-type estimate is interpretable?

historical_evidence.finding: Sequence-level PPP by inferred play type produced SPOT_UP 2.83 PPP and TRANSITION 0.62 PPP, caused by an assisted flag that exists only on makes; after the classifier was rewritten, SPOT_UP was about 1.16 and TRANSITION about 1.20. Recorded failure mechanism: C_artifact. Sample not recorded.

Foul-ending share and PPP by play type showed OTHER with 36% of possessions ending in fouls and inflated PPP (FOUL_BUCKET); DRIVE was 12pp below the foul benchmark (FOUL_LEAK); PNR had a 22% foul rate; only 335 of 50,668 possessions (0.7%) mapped to a real play type via initiation_type.

Label accuracy and distribution audit failed overall: OTHER 20.2% against a target below 10%; 40.8% of labels low confidence; DRIVE foul-draw 1.7% against a 14-22% benchmark; most play types above the PPP benchmark band; MIA identity checks failed. Verdict recorded as tool_eval_fail.

Backfill verification over 921,514 possessions failed: PNR 28.7% against a 20-28% band; PULL_UP 7.9%; 3,100 games with team PNR above 33%; team identity failed; 82.8% of PNR labels were proxy_calibrated; PNR PPP 0.948 passed; temporal check passed. Final result FAIL.

Shot-level PNR share of half-court shots varied from about 7.6% (OKC) and 7.9% (BOS) to 13.8% (IND), with no pass/fail gate. The rates were used as a calibration input for PBPProxyPNR, and later logs show calibrated PNR at about 17.9-19.6% of possessions.
On-ball coverage labels were confident for only 14.9% of DET on-ball possessions (10 of 67) and 3.3% of ORL possessions (2 of 60). switches_on was unpopulated. Verdict recorded as failed_gate.

Playoff series-progression PPP was pooled over 1,197 records with no CIs. DRIVE rose from 0.889 to 0.949 and PNR rose by 0.087. Recorded as no clear signal, with selection and regression-to-the-mean caveats.

DRIVE PPP was 1.198 in the regular season and 0.912 in the playoffs (-0.286 across 25 teams); PNR was -0.173 and PULL_UP +0.301. Motivated the playoff DRIVE exclusion. Cells had at least 30 possessions and no CIs were recorded.

Defensive PPP allowed and possession share, regular season versus playoffs: DRIVE allowed fell from 1.191 to 0.923 and PNR share rose 12.1pp. The record notes the PNR share jump may reflect tagging differences. Verdict descriptive.

Player routing V4 versus V5 gave 8 divergences with 0 scoreable, because 8 players were missing from Neo4j. Recorded as A_unanswerable and inconclusive; included only as an example of graph-database coverage gaps.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Sequence-level PPP computed on play types inferred from play-by-play, before the classifier was corrected
failed_approaches.why: An assisted flag present only on makes created an apparent effect (SPOT_UP 2.83 PPP) that disappeared after the rewrite (about 1.16). Recorded as C_artifact.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Per-play-type PPP comparison using initiation_type-based labels
failed_approaches.why: Foul endings inflated OTHER PPP, DRIVE foul rates were implausibly low, and only 0.7% of possessions mapped to a real play type. Recorded as C_artifact.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Label accuracy and distribution audit of inferred play types
failed_approaches.why: Foul leakage into OTHER, 40.8% low-confidence labels and failed identity checks; recorded as LIM:label_or_classification_error, LIM:leakage and LIM:small_sample.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Play-type label backfill verification across 921,514 possessions
failed_approaches.why: Distribution and team-identity checks failed, and most PNR labels were proxy-calibrated (82.8%). Final FAIL.

failed_approaches.what_failed: On-ball defensive scheme labeling from matchup data
failed_approaches.why: Only 3.3% to 14.9% of possessions received confident labels, and switches_on was not populated. Recorded as failed_gate.

evidence_establishes: The retrieved records establish that play-type labels built from this play-by-play have repeatedly failed validation: foul leakage into OTHER and DRIVE, PNR proxy calibration, implausible PULL_UP shares, and team identity failures.
Sequence-level PPP computed on inferred labels has already produced a confirmed artifact (SF-PAP-096), so an unvalidated teammate-DRIVE-to-PNR comparison carries a documented risk of the same kind.
Playoff and regular-season play-type PPP differ materially (SF-APPS-011), so pooling playoff data into a regular-season-style test is risky.
Within the returned records, no study tests a sequential teammate-DRIVE-before-PNR effect on PNR PPP.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether a teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR changes PNR PPP. No returned record tests this sequence, and none reports a sequential effect.
The true PNR or DRIVE labeling accuracy after the current classifier fixes. The records describe earlier versions, and the status of the corrected classifier is not recorded.
Any valid effect size, confidence interval or sample size for the sequence. The records mostly lack CIs and power calculations.
Whether the 2025-26 playoff data, which were partial before 2026-06-21, can be used at the question date of 2026-06-14.
own_inferences: The question says 'any' teammate DRIVE, which is an unconditional claim with no stated window, so the sequence definition (same possession, prior possession, or within N seconds) must be fixed before any test. The records do not show how the earlier studies defined sequence.

The sequence and the PNR outcome may both depend on the same labeling pipeline. If DRIVE and PNR labels come from the same inferrer, misclassification may be correlated and could produce spurious sequence effects, as in SF-PAP-096.
Obvious confounders include game state, shot clock, lineup quality, the ball-handler and screener pair, and the defense's coverage scheme, none of which the records address.
Data version matters. The question date is before the 2025-26 playoffs are complete, so those games must be excluded or the cut-off must be documented.
uncertainties: The retrieval returned no record that directly tests the teammate-DRIVE-to-PNR relationship, so the historical base is indirect.
The current status of the label fixes (SF-PAP-096 rewrite, SF-APPA-030 proxy calibration) is not recorded.
Sample sizes for DRIVE-then-PNR sequences are not recorded in any returned record.
Several records have no CIs or sample sizes, so their effects cannot be used to estimate power.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieved records show repeated, documented play-type labeling artifacts, including a sequence-level PPP artifact (SF-PAP-096) and failed label audits (SF-APPM-014, SF-APPA-030). These make a direct test on the current labels unreliable. The decision therefore moves from a direct test to do_not_proceed until labels pass validation gates. The historical evidence did not establish any sequence effect in either direction.

blocking_constraints.text: DRIVE and PNR labels are derived from play-by-play outcomes, so the sequence test can condition on the outcome that defines the PPP label.
Play-type labels have failed audits for foul leakage, PNR proxy calibration and identity checks; no validated label set is recorded.
Labels inferred from full-possession play-by-play may use information that occurs after the sequence being tested.
DRIVE-then-PNR sequence counts are not recorded, and the effect size is unknown, so power cannot be established.
Game state, lineup, matchup and shot-clock effects are not controlled in any returned record.

prior_work.summary: No returned record tests a teammate DRIVE preceding a PNR and its effect on PNR PPP. Earlier records establish label-validity problems (SF-PAP-096, SF-CHT-025, SF-APPM-014, SF-APPA-030), an on-ball labeling gate failure (SF-APPS-058), and a regular-season versus playoff DRIVE PPP difference (SF-APPS-011). They are relevant for risk, not as an answer.

risks.text: Play-type labels have documented foul leakage, PNR proxy calibration (82.8%), implausible PULL_UP shares and identity failures; a sequence built on these labels is not interpretable.
PNR labels are derived from the same play-by-play outcomes as PPP, so the outcome defines the label.
A preceding DRIVE may be tagged using events that occur after the PNR possession starts (SF-APPM-014 records leakage into OTHER).
A prior sequence-level PPP computed on inferred labels produced a construction artifact (SF-PAP-096, artifact_found).
Game state, lineup quality, shot clock and defensive coverage may drive both the DRIVE and PNR PPP without any sequence effect.
Sample sizes for DRIVE-then-PNR sequences are not recorded, and most earlier records lack CIs, so power is unknown.
The graph and derived records cover only part of the possessions (for example the 0.7% initiation_type mapping in SF-CHT-025), so some sequences may be rare or unobserved.
'Any teammate DRIVE' invites many lineup, player and window definitions; without a pre-specified window, post hoc selection is likely.
Regular-season, playoff and partial 2025-26 data differ materially (SF-APPS-011), and the 2025-26 playoffs were incomplete at the question date.
PPP per possession has an unknown reliability for the rare PNR-after-DRIVE subset, and no reliability estimate is recorded.
Sequence detection on the graph may mismatch possessions or players, as in the missing-player routing failure (SF-APPS-009).

design.estimand: Not estimable until labels are validated. Minimum viable estimand: the difference in PNR PPP between possessions preceded by a teammate DRIVE and matched possessions not preceded by one, within a pre-specified window, conditioned on game state, lineup and defensive scheme.
design.unit: Ball-handler PNR possession, with the preceding teammate possession as the exposure.
design.sample: Regular seasons 2022-23 to 2024-25 and the 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13). Exclude the 2025-26 playoffs, which were partial before 2026-06-21. Playoffs for 2022-23 to 2024-25 may be analysed separately, not pooled with regular-season data.
design.power: Not computable from the records. Before any test, count DRIVE-then-PNR sequences by team and season and run a pre-analysis power calculation using the 2024-25 PNR PPP variance. If the minimum detectable effect is above a pre-registered threshold, the test does not proceed.
design.controls: Label validation first: hand-check a random sample of DRIVE and PNR labels against video or tracking data and require pass thresholds on foul rate, PNR share and team identity. Then adjust for score margin, period, clock, lineup, shot-clock remaining, the screener and ball-handler pair, and opponent defensive scheme (where the matchup feed is populated). Use leave-one-season-out checks.
design.falsification: A placebo sequence (a teammate PULL_UP or SPOT_UP preceding PNR) and a shuffled-possession-order placebo should show no effect. Any sequence effect that also appears in the placebo or disappears after the label-validation step counts as an artifact, as in SF-PAP-096.
design.multiplicity: Pre-register one primary window and one primary sequence definition. Treat all other windows, play-type predecessors and team splits as exploratory with a correction for multiple comparisons (for example Holm).
design.decision_rule: Proceed to the primary test only if (a) label validation passes all pre-registered gates, (b) the sequence count meets the pre-computed power threshold, and (c) the placebo shows no effect. Report a supported effect only if the CI excludes zero after adjustment and it survives the placebo. Otherwise report inconclusive or artifact, not a causal claim.
design.data_version: Data snapshot as of 2026-06-14. Use regular-season 2022-23 to 2025-26 (2025-26 complete from 2026-04-13) and playoffs 2022-23 to 2024-25 only. Freeze the label-classifier version and record its hash before analysis.

methodological_questions: Does a teammate drive before a pick-and-roll raise PNR points per possession?
Can play-type labels derived from play-by-play be validated and are they free of outcome leakage?
What sample size, exposure, and confounding risks affect a test of sequential play-type effects?

You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
